prompt: How much do the copied events overstate MRR on 2025-06-30? These tables may hold errors. Some subscription events arrived twice: two rows of subscription_events are copies of one event when subscription_id, event_type, event_date and mrr_delta_local all match. Keep the row with the lowest event_id. Clean nothing else. A subscription's MRR on a date is the sum of its mrr_delta_local with event_date on or before that date, in its own currency as the rows hold it; do not convert. For each subscription with at least one copy among its events dated on or before 2025-06-30, return three columns, in this order: subscription_id, mrr_with_copies (the sum over every row that arrived) and mrr (the sum once copies are removed). Return one row for each such subscription. Any row order is fine.
hints: Next, number the copies of each event dated up to 2025-06-30, then per subscription add up mrr_delta_local over every row and over the rows numbered 1.
Keep only the subscriptions where a copy arrived: their row count is above their count of rows numbered 1.
why_this_works: Summing every row and only the rows numbered 1 per subscription shows how far the copies push MRR up, and HAVING keeps the subscriptions with a copy.
